finding: §4.2 never names which component writes `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`, and both candidates contradict another section. If the driver writes it, its `summary` cannot contain "the gate's own output when a gate failed" — the gate runs inside the child and its output exists only in the child's `.jsonl` log, which §3.1 step 5 and §3.5 forbid the driver from reading beyond the single spend key (Non-Goal 6). If the child's `tp done` writes it, then §5.2's rule that an escalating unit "does not set `last_failure`" and the driver-side clearing on a matching `(unit_kind, unit_id)` success are being enforced by a component the spec never gives that responsibility to, and a harness crash that never reaches `tp` leaves the non-zero-exit case unwritten.
suggestion: State the writer explicitly and split the two triggers: the child's `tp done` writes `last_failure` on a failed quality gate (it is the only component holding the gate output), and the driver writes it on a non-zero unit exit with a tp-authored summary derived from the exit code, kind and runner command — never from the log. Say which component clears it, and add a §10.3 assertion that a gate-failure summary carries the gate output while a harness-crash summary does not.

finding: §4.2 says tp records `last_failure` when a unit "exits non-zero, or closes with a failed quality gate", but the driver can only observe the first: a gate failure happens inside `tp done` in the child, and the harness around it may still exit 0. So the gate-failure write has to be made by `tp done` itself, and nothing says where it gets `unit_kind`, `unit_id` and `phase` (presumably `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID`/`TP_PHASE`), nor what happens when `tp done`'s gate fails outside a run, where those variables are unset and the file is not run-scoped (`.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`) — an interactive gate failure would leave a record that `tp resume`/`tp brief` then surface to the next unit. Test 23 only exercises the driver path.
suggestion: State that the gate-failure record is written by `tp done` from `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID`/`TP_PHASE`, and that it is written only when those are set (i.e. inside a run); say explicitly whether a non-run gate failure writes nothing. Add a test for a gate failure inside a child and one outside a run.

finding: Test 5 asserts concurrency "from the seam's recorded spawn and exit timestamps". A fake runner that exits immediately can produce identical timestamps for two sequential spawns at any clock granularity, so the positive half (role units *do* overlap) passes on a serial implementation, and the negative half (other kinds never overlap) is a claim about the absence of an interval — both are flaky rather than deterministic. This is the one test in §10 whose verdict depends on scheduling.
suggestion: Replace the timestamp comparison with a barrier the seam controls: have concurrent role children block on a rendezvous file/counter that only releases once N siblings are in flight (so a serial driver deadlocks or times out and the test fails deterministically), and assert non-overlap of other kinds from a seam-maintained "currently running" counter that must never exceed 1.

finding: Tests 6 and 36 turn on a "crashed driver" / "driver death", and test 35 on the `crashed` run_state, but the spec defines no crash mechanism — and it defines the two obvious signals away: §3.4 makes `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM` graceful stops recorded as `interrupted` (hence `stopped`, not `crashed`). A test author is left to guess `SIGKILL`, a panic, or a hand-truncated run state, and the three choices leave different residue (lock released by the OS vs. held, run row with null `exit_code` vs. none), which is precisely what tests 6, 35 and 36 assert about.
suggestion: Name the fault injection once, in §3.5: a crash is the driver process disappearing without writing `stop_reason` (SIGKILL in tests), the OS releases the run lock, and any in-flight unit rows keep their null `exit_code`. Reference that definition from tests 6, 35 and 36.

finding: Nothing says what happens when `runner.cmd` does not exist on PATH or is not executable. §3.2.1 makes an unresolvable placeholder a usage error "before any child is spawned", but an exec failure is discovered at spawn time, so under the current text it becomes an ordinary failed attempt: every retry fails identically, the run ends with `unit-failure` (exit 4), and the operator gets no statement that the harness itself was missing. That is the most likely first-run misconfiguration of the whole feature.
suggestion: Preflight `runner.cmd` (and each per-kind map entry's `cmd`) for existence/executability before the loop starts and make a failure a usage error (exit 2) naming the command, or define a dedicated `stop_reason` for it; add it to §10.2's runner tests.

finding: Two normative claims in §3.2.1 have no test in §10. (a) "Every child is spawned with stdin closed" — a §2 lesson row (backgrounded runs hang on stdin) and the hardest unattended failure to diagnose, yet nothing asserts it. (b) The built-in templates' contents: the `claude` arg vector, the `opencode` arg vector, and the rule that the `--max-budget-usd` pair is dropped at 0 for `claude` while a positional template receives a literal `0`. Test 10 only says placeholders resolve and test 11 only covers `spend_key` absence, so an implementation that always passes `--max-budget-usd 0` passes every listed test.
suggestion: Add to §10.2: a test that a child's stdin is closed (the seam reports EOF on a read rather than blocking), and a test that resolves both built-in templates at `run_max_unit_budget_usd` 0 and non-zero, asserting the exact argv in all four combinations.

finding: §3.2.1 says an unresolvable placeholder is "a usage error (exit 2) raised before any child is spawned", and test 10 asserts exactly that — but §3.2 allows `runner` to be a per-kind map whose `audit-role` entry is only reached in a later iteration. The spec never says the driver validates every entry of the map (and every entry's placeholders) at start, so one engineer writes a test where a broken `audit-role` template fails at startup and another writes one where it fails on dispatch, mid-run, after implement units already ran. Test 56 has the same hole for the two shape errors (map without `default`, runner object without `cmd`): §3.2 calls them usage errors but never says when they are detected, and §3.4 only assigns exit 2 to "a usage error before the loop starts".
suggestion: State in §3.2 that the whole `runner` value — every map entry, its `cmd`, and every placeholder in every entry's `args` — is resolved and validated once at run start, before the first child, and that a failure there is exit 2 with no run state written. Then extend tests 10 and 56 to a per-kind map whose non-first-kind entry is broken and assert the failure happens before any child is spawned.

finding: The driver "reads one number from the final line of that unit's log", but §3.5 redirects the child's stdout **and** stderr into that one `.jsonl` file, so the final line is frequently a stderr line (a runner warning, a shell diagnostic) rather than the runner's result object. The spec never says what happens when the final line is not JSON, or parses but lacks the declared `spend_key`: is that `spend: null` for the unit (like a runner declaring no key), or a failed attempt? An implementer must invent the rule, and it directly changes whether `cap-budget` accrues.
suggestion: Define the fallback explicitly: scan backwards for the last line that parses as JSON and contains `spend_key` (bounded to the last N lines), and treat "not found" as `spend: null` for that unit — never as a failed attempt — reporting it once in the run state. Add a test with trailing stderr noise after the runner's final result line.

finding: "A unit is attempted `1 + run_max_unit_retries` times" never says *when* the extra attempt happens: inside the same iteration (before §3.1 step 5 re-reads cycle state) or as a fresh iteration after re-polling the oracle. With parallel role units it also does not say whether a sibling that exhausts its attempts stops the run immediately while other roles are still in flight, or whether the driver joins the whole concurrent set first. §3.4's "children already spawned run to completion" covers caps and signals, not this. Test 8 counts attempts and test 5 asserts overlap, but neither pins the schedule, so two implementations both pass while behaving differently on the failure path.
suggestion: Add one sentence: retries are scheduled within the same iteration, immediately after the failed attempt (so the role's deleted-file precondition in §3.1.1 still holds), and the driver joins every child of a concurrent set before deciding `unit-failure`.

finding: "Caps are evaluated between iterations only. Children already spawned run to completion, so a run can overshoot its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration" names only wall-clock and budget, but `run_max_units` overshoots on exactly the same terms: an iteration that spawns five concurrent role units can push the attempt count past `run_max_units` mid-set. The spec never says whether the driver spawns the whole set anyway or trims it to the remaining budget, and test 33 (all three counters agree) is satisfied either way.
suggestion: Name `cap-units` in the overshoot sentence and state the rule — the driver spawns a concurrent set whole and checks `run_max_units` only between iterations, so units may overshoot by at most one set.

finding: Round 15's log-ownership settlement makes the driver redirect each child's stdout/stderr to $TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl and resolves {log_path} to that same file, so a runner that writes its own log now has a second, independent handle on a file the driver is already writing. No ordering or open-mode rule is stated (append vs truncate, interleaving at independent offsets), which undercuts unchanged §3.2.2's requirement that the driver read one number from 'the final line of that unit's log' — the final line is no longer well-defined. §3.2.1's TP_RUNNER_SEAM is the concrete instance: the fake runner is handed {log_path} and 'writes a final log line carrying that key' while its stdout is redirected to the same path, so the spend/budget-cap tests depend on undefined write behaviour.
suggestion: State the writer contract in §3.5: either the driver's redirect is the sole writer and {log_path} is passed only so a runner can point its own logging at it in append mode (O_APPEND, no truncate), with the driver reading the last parseable line rather than the last byte-run; or keep the runner's log separate and have the driver read spend from that path. Mirror whichever rule is chosen in §3.2.1's seam description and in test 60.

finding: The log path is `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`, but §3.1.1 defines a unit `id` as free-form durable subject text: `role:item_id` for `audit-fix` (contains a colon), a spec base name for `review-resolve`/`decompose`, and a task id for `implement`. No sanitization, escaping or length rule is given, so tests 17 and 60 cannot be written deterministically for an `audit-fix` unit — two engineers will disagree on whether the file is `3-audit-fix-go-safety:item-7.jsonl`, a sanitized form, or a hashed one, and a colon is not a portable filename character.
suggestion: Pin the transform in §3.5: name the exact character class allowed in the path component and the substitution for everything else (e.g. every character outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` becomes `-`), plus a max length. Add an assertion to test 60 that an `audit-fix` unit whose id contains `:` produces the documented path and that `{log_path}` expands to that same string.

finding: `--status` must report `in_flight` vs `crashed` from whether `.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock` is held — "the lock is the only evidence separating the last two" — while the same section states "Neither sub-mode takes the run lock" (and test 58 asserts it). With flock the only portable way to learn that a lock is held is a non-blocking acquire, which does take it, briefly; during that window a legitimately starting `tp run` would see the lock held and exit 4. The implementer has to guess whether a try-acquire-and-release counts as "taking" the lock and whether the spurious exit 4 is acceptable.
suggestion: Say that `--status` probes with a non-blocking acquire it releases immediately, that "takes the run lock" in test 58 means "does not hold it for the duration", and either accept or rule out the narrow race with a starting `tp run` (e.g. `tp run` retries the lock once before exiting 4).

finding: `tp resume --json` gains `next_units` (and §4.2 adds `last_failure`), and §4.1 states the driver is the only consumer of `next_units` — it parses `next_units`, `round`, `phase` and nothing else, and it reads them from `--json`. But §6.2 makes the SessionStart hook inject `tp resume --compact` into EVERY child, and claims its size is 'bounded by an existing command's compact output' — a bound that this same version just enlarged. The spec fixes `--compact` semantics only for `tp run --status` (§7: stop_reason and cap totals survive, per-unit rows and log paths stripped) and says nothing about what `tp resume --compact` keeps. If compact carries `next_units`, every unit in the run pays for a machine-only array plus `next_action`, whose `command`/`brief_command`/`payload` render `next_units[0]` by construction — the same brief twice — and a role unit, which is told its unit by its own brief, never reads either.
suggestion: State the compact rule for `tp resume` where `next_units` is defined: `--compact` omits `next_units` (the driver reads `--json`), keeps `next_action` as the human/agent-facing summary, and keeps `last_failure` only if `tp brief` does not already carry it — so the SessionStart payload does not carry the same unit description twice. Add it to test 38 or 27 so the injected payload's contents are asserted rather than assumed.

finding: Test 23 covers `last_failure` only for the "non-zero unit exit" trigger, but §4.2 states two triggers — "exits non-zero, **or** closes with a failed quality gate" — and pins the content rule (`summary` is tp-authored: the failing command plus the gate's own output, never the child's prose). Neither the gate-failure trigger nor the summary-content rule is asserted anywhere, and the gate branch is the one that needs a test most, since it is unstated whether a gate failure that already makes `tp done` exit non-zero is one event or two.
suggestion: Extend test 23 to a unit whose `tp done` fails the quality gate while the harness exits 0, asserting a `last_failure` is written with a tp-authored `summary` containing the failing command and the gate output, and that a child's stdout text never appears in it.

finding: §5.1's fence covers four table rows plus `runner` and `notify_cmd`, and row 4 fences `run_max_*`. But §5.2's `decision` enum is `skip-gate`, `raise-review-cap`, `raise-audit-cap`, `import-force`, `other` — it has no name for a run-cap raise and none for `runner`/`notify_cmd`. A unit refused at row 4 must escalate as `other`, which the spec never states, so test 19 (four operations exit 2 with a hint) and test 22 (the record's contents) cannot agree on what the resulting record carries.
suggestion: Either add `raise-run-cap` to the enum or state explicitly in §5.1 that a refusal outside the three named decisions escalates as `other`, and assert the resulting `decision` value in test 19 or 22 for each refused operation.

finding: §5.2 says a record "that fails schema validation" is judged as an ordinary unit, and test 47 covers only "a unit that wrote a **valid** escalation record" — but validity is never defined. The shape `{decision, unit_kind, unit_id, phase, evidence, options[], at}` does not say which keys are required (the CLI makes `--option` optional, so `options[]` may be absent or `[]`), whether an unknown `decision` value invalidates the record, whether unknown extra keys are tolerated, or whether an unparseable file counts as "wrote none" or as "fails validation". No test exercises the invalid branch at all.
suggestion: Add a required/optional key list and an explicit rule for an out-of-enum `decision`, extra keys, and an unparseable file; then add a test to §10.3 asserting that a record missing a required key, and one with an unknown `decision`, both leave the unit judged by its §3.3 predicate and exit code (and do set `last_failure`).

finding: §6.3 says the `claude` template appends `["--agent", "<name>"]` per unit kind unconditionally, and in the next paragraph that "a runner that cannot load a plugin gets no agent definitions, and the unit runs without them". Those cannot both hold for the `claude` runner: with the plugin absent, `--agent tp-reviewer` names an agent the harness cannot resolve, which fails the invocation rather than degrading. §3.2.1 also enumerates the `claude` template's `args` as a closed list with exactly one conditional append (the budget pair), so the same template's argument vector is defined twice with different content.
suggestion: Make the append conditional and say on what — e.g. the driver appends `--agent` only when the plugin's agent definitions are present (the `SessionStart` preflight already establishes plugin presence), otherwise it omits the flag. Fold the `--agent` append into §3.2.1's enumeration of the `claude` template so one section owns that argument vector, and extend test 44 to assert the flag is absent when no agent definitions are installed.

finding: Test 16 requires each field to "accept both range endpoints, and reject one step outside each", but two §7 fields are decimal dollars (`run_max_budget_usd` 0-10000, `run_max_unit_budget_usd` 0-1000) and the spec fixes no precision, so "one step outside" is undefined — 10000.01, 10000.001 and 10000.0000001 are three different tests. The 0 endpoint compounds it: for both budget fields 0 means *disabled* (§3.4, §5.1), so "the low endpoint" is a mode switch rather than a magnitude, and the test cannot say whether a negative value, or a value between 0 and the smallest meaningful cent, is a range error or a disable.
suggestion: State the accepted precision for the two budget fields (e.g. two decimal places, values rounded/rejected beyond that) and give the exact rejected probe for each endpoint in test 16 (e.g. -0.01 and 10000.01), plus an explicit statement that 0 is accepted as *disabled* rather than as a range minimum.

finding: `notify_cmd` is specified only as a *read*: "per-operator rather than per-project and is read from `.tp/local.json` only" (§7), and test 16 asserts the read side. No command is named that writes it — `tp set --workflow` writes a task override, and the project config is `.tp/config.json`, neither of which is consulted for this field. Meanwhile §5.1 fences a unit from setting `notify_cmd` "at all, at any layer", which presumes a write path exists to fence. An implementer cannot both ship the fence and leave the field unwritable.
suggestion: Name the supported write path (e.g. `tp config --local notify_cmd=…`, alongside whatever writes `.tp/local.json` today for `tp use`), state that `tp set --workflow notify_cmd=` is rejected because the field does not resolve from a task override, and extend test 16 to cover the write.

finding: `location_clusters` entries are `{location, roles[], severities[], count}` with no semantics for any of the three aggregates: `count` may be the number of findings at the location or the number of roles; `roles[]` and `severities[]` may be deduplicated or parallel to the findings; entry and array ordering is unspecified (so a JSON-equality assertion is non-deterministic); and it is unstated whether one role reporting the same location twice contributes to `count` while never forming a cluster. Test 28 exercises only the two-roles-two-classes case, so none of this is pinned.
suggestion: Define each key in §8a.1 (`count` = number of findings at the location; `roles[]` and `severities[]` deduplicated and sorted; clusters sorted by location) and state that same-role repeats never create a cluster. Extend test 28 with a three-finding two-role case asserting the exact object, and a same-role-twice case asserting no cluster.

finding: §8a.3 pins the auto-detect cap at 50 files, and test 30 only asserts that a set "truncated by the cap" reports `truncated` true with `total_changed` above `total_files`. The inclusive/exclusive boundary is untested: a changed set of exactly 50 must report `truncated` false with `total_changed == total_files == 50`, and 51 must report true with `total_files` 50. As written the test passes with a cap of 40 or 60, which is the exact failure mode CLAUDE.md records from v0.34.0 (a documented range verified with a value far from the bound). The spec also never says whether the 50 is configurable, so a test author cannot tell whether to pin the literal.
suggestion: State in §8a.3 that 50 is a fixed literal (or name the field that overrides it), and rewrite test 30 to assert the pair of cases at 50 and 51 with the exact `truncated`, `total_files` and `total_changed` values for each.

finding: Test 15 enumerates four new git-ignored paths and §10.7 says the `.tp/.gitignore` fixture "gains four entries", but §3.1.1 introduces a fifth new artifact under `.tp/` — the run lock at `.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock` — and neither the test nor §10.7 says whether `.tp/locks/` is already ignored or must be added. As written a reviewer cannot judge whether "four entries" is complete. §3.2.2's run-start report (which kinds are unmetered, and that `run_max_budget_usd` is inert for them) is likewise required output with no test.
suggestion: State in §3.1.1 whether `.tp/locks/` is already covered by the shipped `.tp/.gitignore`, and correct the entry count in test 15/§10.7 accordingly; add a §10.2 assertion that a run under a runner with no `spend_key` prints the unmetered-kinds notice once at start.

finding: §5.1 defines unattended mode as active when `TP_UNATTENDED` is "present, non-empty and not `0`", but every test (19, 20, 40) uses the single value `1`. The three off-cases (`0`, empty string, unset) and the surprising on-cases (`false`, `no`, ` `) are unasserted, so an implementation that checks `== "1"` passes the whole suite while silently disabling the fence for any operator who exports `TP_UNATTENDED=true`.
suggestion: Add a table-driven case to test 19 over `1`, `true`, `0`, `""` and unset, asserting active/inactive per §5.1's rule; decide and state whether a whitespace-only value is present-and-non-empty.

finding: Two structural problems make the test list hard to hold stable. (a) §10.5 is titled "Signals the driver reads" (the §8a subjects) but tests 33-40 are loop, run-state, environment and oracle tests belonging to §10.1/§10.2 — so a reader checking "is every §8a claim tested" must filter the section by hand. (b) §6.2 cites "test 52" by ordinal; the numbering is global and unanchored, so inserting any test before it silently re-points the citation to a different assertion. §3.3, §3.5 and §5.2 cite sections rather than ordinals everywhere else.
suggestion: Move tests 33-40 into §10.1/§10.2 (or retitle §10.5), and replace §6.2's "test 52" with a prose reference such as "§10.6's shared-predicate test" so the citation survives renumbering.

finding: §3.1 step 4 says "units marked concurrent together, every other kind alone", which describes concurrency as a property carried on the unit entry. §4.1 states the opposite about the same array: "Concurrency is not repeated per entry — it is fixed per kind by §3.3's table". A reader implementing the loop from §3.1 alone would look for a field on `next_units[i]` that §4.1 deliberately does not define.
suggestion: Reword §3.1 step 4 to derive concurrency from the kind — e.g. "spawn one runner process per unit, running the kinds §3.3 marks parallel together and every other kind alone" — so the array's shape is described identically in both sections.

finding: §3.4 states that because caps are evaluated between iterations only, "a run can overshoot its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration", enumerating two of the three quantitative caps. `run_max_units` overshoots on the same terms and by a larger, structural margin: §3.3 spawns role units concurrently, so an iteration starting one unit below the cap spawns as many children as the phase has active roles. The `cap-units` row ("Spawned children reached `run_max_units`") reads as a hard threshold, which invites an implementation that either counts mid-iteration and truncates a role fan-out — breaking §3.3's parallelism — or silently exceeds a cap the spec presents as exact.
suggestion: Add `run_max_units` to the overshoot sentence and state the bound explicitly: an iteration is never truncated, so the unit count can exceed `run_max_units` by up to the number of concurrent units in the final iteration. Assert the overshoot bound in test 3 alongside the per-cap `stop_reason`.

finding: §3.4's overshoot contract — caps are evaluated between iterations only, already-spawned children run to completion, the driver kills nothing, and a run may exceed its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration — has no test. Test 3 asserts only that each cap yields its own `stop_reason`, which an implementation that kills in-flight children on a wall-clock trip would also satisfy.
suggestion: Add a §10.1 test that trips `run_max_wall_clock_seconds` while a slow seam child is in flight and asserts the child was allowed to exit with its recorded `exit_code`, that no further unit was spawned, and that `totals.wall_clock_seconds` exceeds the cap.

finding: The preflight compares "`plugin.json`'s own version … against `tp --version`" without pinning the parse or the comparison: the output format of `tp --version` is not quoted, and no rule covers a dev build whose version string carries a suffix or lags the tag. During tp's own self-development the standing rule is to run a freshly built binary, so the first dogfooding session of this plugin hits whichever behaviour the implementer picks (fail closed on an unparseable/prerelease version, or pass).
suggestion: Quote the expected `tp --version` output, specify a semver compare on the leading `x.y.z` with any suffix ignored, and state that an unparseable version fails with the install command (so the failure is loud), while a matching-or-newer core version passes regardless of suffix.

finding: §7's last line — "Under `--compact`, `stop_reason` and the cap totals survive; per-unit rows and log paths are stripped" — never names which command takes `--compact` (`tp run --status` is implied but §3.5 lists only `--status` and `--dry-run`), and no §10 test asserts the compact projection. A test author cannot tell whether `tp run --dry-run --compact` and the audit-phase divergence signals are in or out of the surviving set.
suggestion: Move the sentence into §3.5 next to `--status`, name the sub-modes that accept `--compact`, and say whether `run_state` and the divergence signals survive; add a §10.2 test asserting the exact surviving key set.
